meta.title: Snakes & Ladders
meta.subtitle: Harden Google Cloud from IAM & VPC-SC perimeters to Cloud Armor, Binary Authorization, CMEK & Autonomous SecOps.
meta.author: Google Cloud Architecture

1.title: Day-0 Cloud Landing Zone & Identity Baseline
1.quip: "A brand-new Organization node, zero standing keys, and a mission to build an unbreachable zero-trust cloud."
1.tip: Anchor every Google Cloud environment with Workload Identity Federation, Organization Policy guardrails, VPC Service Controls, and centralized Cloud Audit Logs.

100.title: Autonomous Zero-Trust & SecOps Mastery!
100.quip: "Zero static keys, enforced VPC-SC perimeters, KMS-attested containers, and sub-minute autonomous SecOps containment!"
100.tip: Defense-in-depth unites least-privilege IAM, context-aware perimeters, Cloud Armor edge defense, attested supply chains, CMEK/SDP data protection, and continuous SCC Attack Path reduction.

ladders.title: Workload Identity Federation for CI/CD
ladders.quip: "Replaced all long-lived service account JSON keys in GitHub Actions and AWS workloads with OIDC Workload Identity Federation. Eliminated static credential leakage risk across 120 repositories and removed quarterly key rotation toil."
ladders.tip: Use Workload Identity Federation to exchange external IdP OIDC/SAML tokens for short-lived STS credentials instead of exporting service account keys.
ladders.q: How does Workload Identity Federation authenticate external CI/CD pipelines (like GitHub Actions) to Google Cloud without exported JSON keys?
opts: The external IdP issues a signed OIDC token that Google Cloud STS validates against attribute conditions and exchanges for a short-lived access token
It encrypts a long-lived JSON private key inside a public DNS TXT record
It disables IAM authentication on target Google Cloud APIs for external IP ranges
ladders.why: Security Token Service (STS) verifies the external OIDC/SAML assertion against your Workload Identity Pool provider and attribute mappings, issuing ephemeral tokens.

ladders.title: Just-in-Time Elevations with Privileged Access Manager
ladders.quip: "Removed standing production Owner/Admin bindings and deployed Privileged Access Manager (PAM) entitlements with approval workflows. Reduced standing privileged access by 96% while keeping full audit trails and ticket justifications for emergency break-glass access."
ladders.tip: Replace standing privileged IAM bindings with time-bound, approval-gated PAM entitlements and mandatory justification logging.
ladders.q: What primary risk does Privileged Access Manager (PAM) mitigate in production Google Cloud environments?
opts: Network packet loss between on-premises routers and Cloud VPN gateways
Standing over-privileged access, by granting time-bound, audit-logged role elevations only when requested and approved
SQL syntax errors inside Cloud Spanner stored procedures
ladders.why: PAM enforces Just-in-Time (JIT) least privilege with configurable approvers, maximum duration, and Cloud Audit Logs visibility.

ladders.title: Organization-Wide IAM Deny Guardrails
ladders.quip: "Attached an IAM Deny policy at the organization root blocking `iam.serviceAccountKeys.create` and permission changes on audit log sinks for all principals except break-glass admins. Guaranteed that even a compromised Project Owner cannot disable security logging or mint persistent keys."
ladders.tip: IAM Deny policies evaluate before IAM Allow policies and override any grant regardless of role hierarchy.
ladders.q: When both an IAM Allow policy and an IAM Deny policy apply to a principal's API request, how does IAM evaluate access?
opts: Project-level Allow policies override Organization-level Deny policies
IAM prompts the user to solve a CAPTCHA to bypass the Deny rule
IAM Deny policies always take precedence over IAM Allow policies, blocking the action even if the user holds the Organization Administrator or Owner role
ladders.why: In Google Cloud IAM policy evaluation, a matching Deny rule without an satisfied exception immediately denies the request before Allow policies are considered.

ladders.title: VPC Service Controls Enforced Perimeter
ladders.quip: "Promoted the production data warehouse perimeter from dry-run to enforced mode protecting BigQuery, Cloud Storage, and Cloud KMS across 18 projects. Blocked unauthorized data exfiltration to external projects even if a developer's OAuth token is phished."
ladders.tip: VPC Service Controls create a service-level zero-trust boundary around multi-tenant Google Cloud APIs independent of IAM credentials.
ladders.q: Which threat vector does VPC Service Controls specifically stop that IAM least-privilege alone cannot prevent?
opts: An attacker or insider using stolen valid credentials to copy sensitive data from your BigQuery or Cloud Storage bucket into an external Google Cloud project
A brute-force SSH login attempt against an unpatched Linux VM on port 22
Memory corruption inside an unpatched third-party C++ library
ladders.why: VPC-SC restricts Google Cloud API resource movement across perimeter boundaries, preventing exfiltration to unauthorized projects even with valid credentials.

ladders.title: Private Google Access via restricted.googleapis.com
ladders.quip: "Configured internal DNS and VPC routes to send all Google API traffic exclusively to `restricted.googleapis.com` (199.36.153.4/30) with default internet egress removed. Ensured workloads can only reach VPC-SC supported services over Google's private backbone."
ladders.tip: Route private workloads through `restricted.googleapis.com` so non-VPC-SC compliant APIs are blocked at the network layer.
ladders.q: Why should security-sensitive VPC networks route Google API traffic to `restricted.googleapis.com` (199.36.153.4/30) instead of `private.googleapis.com`?
opts: `restricted.googleapis.com` disables TLS encryption to reduce CPU overhead
`restricted.googleapis.com` only exposes Google Cloud APIs that support VPC Service Controls, blocking unsupported APIs that could serve as exfiltration channels
`private.googleapis.com` is only accessible from public IPv6 addresses
ladders.why: Using `restricted.googleapis.com` ensures private workloads can only communicate with services governed by VPC Service Controls.

ladders.title: Context-Aware Access with Chrome Enterprise & BeyondCorp
ladders.quip: "Bound Access Context Manager (ACM) access levels requiring OS patch compliance, hardware-backed device certificates, and corporate IP/geo posture to VPC-SC ingress rules. Stopped unmanaged personal devices from querying production APIs even with valid corporate SSO sessions."
ladders.tip: Combine identity with device posture and IP context via Access Context Manager for BeyondCorp zero-trust enforcement.
ladders.q: How does Access Context Manager (ACM) strengthen VPC Service Controls and Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP)?
opts: By automatically rewriting Python 2 code into Python 3
By replacing BGP route advertisements on Cloud Router
By evaluating fine-grained request attributes such as device encryption status, OS version, client certificate, and source IP before granting access
ladders.why: ACM defines reusable context-aware access levels based on user identity, device posture (Endpoint Verification), and network origin.

ladders.title: Cloud Armor Adaptive Protection Auto-Mitigation
ladders.quip: "Enabled Cloud Armor Adaptive Protection with automated rule deployment on the global External Application Load Balancer. Detected and mitigated a 450,000 RPS Layer-7 botnet flood at Google's edge in under 30 seconds with zero backend saturation."
ladders.tip: Cloud Armor Adaptive Protection uses ML baselines per backend service to fingerprint anomalous L7 attacks and synthesize signature rules.
ladders.q: What does Google Cloud Armor Adaptive Protection do when it detects an anomalous Layer-7 HTTP flood against a load-balanced backend?
opts: It analyzes traffic deviations against ML baselines, alerts SCC/Cloud Monitoring, and generates a tailored WAF signature rule that can be auto-deployed at the edge
It shuts down the entire Google Cloud project to save billing costs
It migrates backend databases from Cloud SQL to local SQLite
ladders.why: Adaptive Protection profiles normal traffic patterns per backend service and generates targeted edge rules matching the attack signature.

ladders.title: Preconfigured OWASP ModSecurity CRS WAF Rules
ladders.quip: "Deployed tuned Cloud Armor preconfigured WAF rules (`sqli-v33-stable`, `xss-v33-stable`, `lfi-v33-stable`, `rce-v33-stable`) at sensitivity level 2. Blocked automated SQLi and remote code execution payloads at the global Anycast edge before reaching GKE ingress pods."
ladders.tip: Use Cloud Armor preconfigured WAF rules with sensitivity tuning and targeted field exclusions to block OWASP Top 10 exploits at the edge.
ladders.q: How do you reduce false positives on a specific JSON request header when using Cloud Armor preconfigured OWASP SQLi/XSS WAF rules?
opts: Disable HTTPS on the Load Balancer so payloads arrive in plaintext
Configure target field exclusions (such as specific request headers, cookies, or query parameters) on the preconfigured WAF rule expression rather than disabling the entire rule
Delete the Cloud Armor security policy and rely on client-side JavaScript validation
ladders.why: Cloud Armor allows excluding specific request fields (headers, cookies, args, URIs) from inspection for a given preconfigured WAF rule ID.

ladders.title: Zero-Trust Internal Apps via Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP)
ladders.quip: "Decommissioned legacy VPN concentrators and placed internal admin dashboards behind Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) with signed JWT verification. Verified every single HTTP request for user identity and device posture without exposing internal network subnets."
ladders.tip: Identity-Aware Proxy shifts access control from network perimeter VPNs to verified per-request identity and context.
ladders.q: Why must backend applications behind Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) validate the `x-goog-iap-jwt-assertion` header in addition to firewall rules?
opts: The header contains the user's plaintext password for database login
Validating the header compresses response images by 80%
Cryptographic JWT signature verification ensures requests cannot bypass IAP if a firewall rule is misconfigured or if another workload inside the VPC attempts lateral spoofing
ladders.why: Verifying the signed IAP JWT guarantees defense-in-depth so even internal lateral traffic or firewall drift cannot spoof authenticated identity.

ladders.title: Binary Authorization with KMS Cryptographic Attestors
ladders.quip: "Enforced Binary Authorization on all production GKE and Cloud Run deployments requiring Cloud Build provenance and vulnerability scan attestations signed by Cloud KMS. Blocked 100% of unsigned, hand-built, or critically vulnerable container images at admission time."
ladders.tip: Use Binary Authorization with KMS-backed attestors and image digests (`@sha256:...`) to enforce supply-chain integrity at deployment admission.
ladders.q: How does Binary Authorization guarantee that only verified container builds can run in a production GKE cluster?
opts: An admission controller verifies that the image digest carries cryptographic attestations signed by trusted Cloud KMS keys from CI/CD and vulnerability checks before scheduling pods
It checks whether the Docker image tag ends with the string `:latest-prod`
It scans container source code only after the container has been running for 30 days
ladders.why: Binary Authorization validates cryptographic signatures (attestations) tied to the immutable image digest before allowing pod admission.

ladders.title: GKE Workload Identity Pod-Level IAM
ladders.quip: "Migrated every GKE cluster from node-level Compute Engine default service accounts to Workload Identity federation for GKE. Scoped IAM permissions strictly per Kubernetes ServiceAccount and blocked pods from querying node metadata credentials."
ladders.tip: Use Workload Identity on GKE so each Kubernetes ServiceAccount authenticates as a distinct, least-privilege IAM principal.
ladders.q: What security boundary does GKE Workload Identity establish inside a multi-tenant Kubernetes cluster?
opts: It gives every pod in the cluster root SSH access to the control plane

It binds individual Kubernetes ServiceAccounts to specific IAM principals (or IAM roles directly) and intercepts the GKE metadata server so pods cannot steal the underlying VM node's service account token
It stores exported JSON keys inside Kubernetes ConfigMaps
ladders.why: Workload Identity replaces shared node-level service accounts with pod-scoped identity federation via the GKE metadata server.

ladders.title: Shielded GKE Nodes with vTPM & Integrity Monitoring
ladders.quip: "Enabled Shielded GKE Nodes with Secure Boot, virtual Trusted Platform Module (vTPM), and Integrity Monitoring across all node pools. Cryptographically verified node boot sequences and prevented kernel-level rootkits or unsigned bootloaders from joining the cluster."
ladders.tip: Always enable Shielded GKE Nodes with Secure Boot and Integrity Monitoring to protect against boot- and kernel-level compromise.
ladders.q: How do Shielded GKE Nodes protect against persistent boot-level or kernel-level rootkits on cluster worker nodes?
opts: By restarting all containers every 5 minutes
By blocking all HTTPS traffic on port 443
Secure Boot verifies digital signatures of all boot components, while vTPM-backed Integrity Monitoring measures the boot sequence against a known-good baseline and alerts on tampering
ladders.why: Shielded GKE Nodes combine UEFI Secure Boot, vTPM measured boot, and continuous Integrity Monitoring reported to Cloud Monitoring/SCC.

ladders.title: Cloud KMS Autokey with Separation of Duties
ladders.quip: "Adopted Cloud KMS Autokey across folders so Terraform provisions dedicated Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK) in a centralized key project automatically. Achieved 100% CMEK coverage with automated 90-day rotation and strict separation between Key Admins and Resource Admins."
ladders.tip: Use Cloud KMS Autokey to automate per-resource CMEK provisioning while enforcing centralized key governance and rotation.
ladders.q: How does Cloud KMS Autokey preserve security separation of duties while letting application teams provision CMEK-protected resources?
opts: Autokey creates and manages keys in a centralized KMS admin project with enforced rotation and IAM policies, while granting resource projects only the CryptoKey Encrypter/Decrypter bindings needed
Autokey grants every application developer Organization Administrator permissions
Autokey stores plaintext AES keys inside the application git repository
ladders.why: KMS Autokey automates least-privilege CMEK creation in a dedicated security project without giving developers direct administrative control over keys.

ladders.title: Sovereign Encryption with Cloud External Key Manager (EKM)
ladders.quip: "Integrated Cloud EKM over Private Service Connect with an external HSM key appliance for regulated financial datasets in BigQuery and Compute Engine. Met strict data sovereignty mandates with externally held keys and cryptographic justification audit logs via Key Access Justifications."
ladders.tip: Pair Cloud EKM with Key Access Justifications when regulatory compliance requires holding encryption keys outside Google Cloud.
ladders.q: When Cloud EKM is paired with Key Access Justifications (KAJ), what control does the customer's external key manager gain?
opts: It bypasses all BigQuery SQL syntax validation

Every wrap/unwrap request from Google Cloud includes a machine-readable justification code (e.g., `CUSTOMER_INITIATED_ACCESS`), allowing the external key manager to automatically approve or deny decryption
It replicates plaintext database rows to public object storage
ladders.why: Key Access Justifications attach a verified reason to every EKM cryptographic request so policy engines can enforce automated approval or denial.

ladders.title: Sensitive Data Protection (DLP) Format-Preserving Tokenization
ladders.quip: "Built a Sensitive Data Protection (Cloud DLP) inspection and de-identification pipeline using KMS-wrapped CryptoDeterministicConfig surrogates before analytics ingestion. De-identified 4 billion customer records while preserving referential integrity for BigQuery JOINs without exposing raw PII."
ladders.tip: Use Sensitive Data Protection deterministic cryptographic tokenization (`CryptoDeterministicConfig`) to enable analytics on sensitive identifiers without exposing cleartext PII.
ladders.q: Which Sensitive Data Protection (Cloud DLP) transformation allows analysts to `JOIN` tables on a sensitive identifier (like SSN or email) without revealing the original value?
opts: Replacing every sensitive value with a single static string `[REDACTED]`
Deleting all primary and foreign key columns from the table
Deterministic encryption (`CryptoDeterministicConfig`) using a KMS-wrapped key and surrogate infoType, which produces repeatable ciphertext tokens for identical inputs
ladders.why: `CryptoDeterministicConfig` generates consistent pseudonymous tokens for identical cleartext values, preserving joinability and distinct counts safely.

ladders.title: SCC Attack Path Simulation & Toxic Combination Remediation
ladders.quip: "Used Security Command Center (SCC) Virtual Red Teaming and Attack Path Simulation to identify an internet-exposed VM with an overly permissive service account reaching a high-value BigQuery dataset. Broke 14 multi-step attack paths and lowered the highest risk exposure score from 9.8 to 0 before any exploitation occurred."
ladders.tip: Prioritize remediation using SCC Attack Path Simulation and Toxic Combinations rather than sorting vulnerabilities by CVSS score in isolation.
ladders.q: How does Security Command Center (SCC) Attack Path Simulation determine which misconfigurations or CVEs pose the highest real-world risk?
opts: It models graph relationships across network reachability, vulnerabilities, IAM bindings, and IAM impersonation chains to simulate how an attacker could reach designated High-Value Resource sets
It sorts findings alphabetically by the name of the Compute Engine instance
It only scans resources between midnight and 1:00 AM on Sundays
ladders.why: SCC's graph-based simulation combines network exposure, CVEs, and IAM blast radius (toxic combinations) to calculate an Attack Exposure Score toward high-value assets.

ladders.title: Real-Time Event & Container Threat Detection
ladders.quip: "Enabled Security Command Center Event Threat Detection (ETD) and Container Threat Detection (CTD) streaming findings to Pub/Sub and Cloud Run remediation functions. Detected and quarantined an unauthorized cryptomining binary and anomalous IAM token minting in under 45 seconds."
ladders.tip: Enable Event Threat Detection (analyzing Cloud Audit/VPC Flow/DNS logs) and Container Threat Detection (kernel-level container runtime monitoring) for real-time breach detection.
ladders.q: How does Container Threat Detection in Security Command Center detect malicious activity inside running GKE pods without requiring agents inside application containers?
opts: It requires developers to paste their source code into a weekly email
It instruments the GKE node OS kernel directly to monitor system calls (`execve`, `memfd_create`, reverse shells, binary drift) and correlates them with container metadata
It only inspects static Dockerfile comments before build time
ladders.why: Container Threat Detection operates at the GKE host kernel level, capturing runtime executions, added binaries, and container escapes without user-space tampering.

ladders.title: Autonomous Threat Hunting with Google SecOps & YARA-L
ladders.quip: "Ingested Cloud Audit Logs, DNS logs, VPC Flow Logs, and EDR telemetry into Google SecOps (Chronicle) with curated YARA-L multi-event correlation rules and SOAR playbooks. Correlated 12 months of petabyte-scale telemetry in sub-second searches and automated compromised session revocation."
ladders.tip: Stream unified cloud and identity telemetry into Google SecOps (Chronicle) to run multi-stage YARA-L detections and automated SOAR containment.
ladders.q: What makes YARA-L 2.0 rules in Google SecOps (Chronicle) uniquely suited for detecting sophisticated cloud identity attacks?
opts: YARA-L only matches static MD5 hashes of Windows `.exe` files on floppy disks
YARA-L disables Cloud Audit Logs to save storage space
YARA-L correlates multiple UDM (Unified Data Model) events over sliding time windows with entity context graphs and threat intelligence indicators
ladders.why: YARA-L operates over Chronicle's Unified Data Model (UDM) and Entity Graph to correlate multi-stage identity, network, and endpoint events.

snakes.title: Exported Service Account JSON Key Leaked in Public Git Repo
snakes.quip: "A developer exported a user-managed service account JSON key with `roles/editor` and accidentally committed it to a public GitHub repository. Automated bots scraped the key within 90 seconds and launched 64 GPU instances across 6 regions for cryptomining."
snakes.tip: User-managed service account keys are bearer credentials that bypass interactive MFA and live indefinitely until revoked.
snakes.prevent: Enforce `constraints/iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation` across the organization and use Workload Identity Federation.
snakes.detect: SCC Event Threat Detection `iam_anomalous_grant` / leaked credential notifications and GitHub Secret Scanning partner alerts.
snakes.recover: Immediately disable and delete the compromised key ID, revoke active tokens, terminate rogue VMs, and audit Cloud Audit Logs by `principalEmail` and `authenticationInfo.serviceAccountKeyName`.
snakes.docLabel: Best Practices for Service Account Keys
snakes.q: What is the most effective preventive control to stop developers from downloading persistent service account JSON keys across a Google Cloud Organization?
opts: Ask developers to rename `.json` key files to `.txt` before committing to Git
Enforce the `constraints/iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation` boolean Organization Policy constraint and adopt Workload Identity Federation or service account impersonation
Rotate the root domain DNS registrar every week
snakes.why: Enforcing `iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation` blocks creation of new user-managed keys organization-wide while encouraging short-lived token patterns.

snakes.title: Default Compute Service Account Left with Project Editor Role
snakes.quip: "Production VMs ran using the default Compute Engine service account (`-compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com`) with the automatic `roles/editor` binding. An SSRF vulnerability on a single web VM allowed the attacker to query `169.254.169.254` and gain read/write access to every storage bucket and database in the project."
snakes.tip: The default Compute Engine service account with `roles/editor` turns any single VM compromise or SSRF into a full project takeover.
snakes.prevent: Enforce `constraints/iam.automaticIamGrantsForDefaultServiceAccounts` and attach dedicated, single-purpose service accounts with predefined/custom least-privilege roles to each workload.
snakes.detect: IAM Recommender excess permission insights and SCC Attack Path Simulation toxic combination findings.
snakes.recover: Attach a dedicated least-privilege service account to the workload, remove `roles/editor` from the default service account, and review IAM Recommender prior usage.
snakes.q: Why is running workloads under the default Compute Engine service account with `roles/editor` considered a critical cloud security anti-pattern?
opts: The default service account cannot authenticate to any Google Cloud API
It limits the VM to a maximum of 1 vCPU
Any workload or SSRF vulnerability that can reach the local metadata server (`169.254.169.254`) inherits broad modify/delete permissions across almost all resources in the project
snakes.why: Granting `roles/editor` to a VM's attached service account massively expands the blast radius of any application compromise or SSRF exploit.

snakes.title: Customer Invoices Exposed via allUsers on Cloud Storage Bucket
snakes.quip: "An engineer troubleshooting a 403 error granted `allUsers` the `roles/storage.objectViewer` role on a bucket storing PDF billing statements. External search indexers enumerated 1.2 million customer invoice PDFs before security teams noticed."
snakes.tip: Never use `allUsers` or `allAuthenticatedUsers` on buckets containing private or internal data; use signed URLs or IAP instead.
snakes.prevent: Enforce Public Access Prevention (`enforced` at org/bucket level) and `constraints/iam.allowedPolicyMemberDomains`.
snakes.detect: Security Command Center `PUBLIC_BUCKET_ACL` findings and Cloud Audit Logs `SetIamPolicy` alerts.
snakes.recover: Enable Public Access Prevention immediately on the bucket, remove `allUsers`/`allAuthenticatedUsers` bindings, and review Data Access audit logs for external IP reads.
snakes.q: Note that `allAuthenticatedUsers` in Google Cloud IAM is often misunderstood. Who is included in the `allAuthenticatedUsers` principal?
opts: Anyone on the internet signed into ANY personal Gmail, Google Workspace, or Google Cloud account worldwide—not just users in your organization
Only employees authenticated via your company's corporate SAML identity provider
Only service accounts inside the same VPC network
snakes.why: `allAuthenticatedUsers` grants access to every Google account holder globally, so it must be treated as public access.

snakes.title: Enforced VPC-SC Without Dry-Run Broke Multi-Project CI/CD
snakes.quip: "The security team switched a VPC Service Controls perimeter straight to Enforced mode on Friday afternoon without analyzing Dry-Run audit logs first. Cloud Build pipelines in the shared DevOps project were immediately blocked from pushing artifacts to Artifact Registry and deploying to GKE inside the perimeter."
snakes.tip: Always validate VPC-SC perimeters in Dry-Run mode first and configure explicit Ingress/Egress rules for cross-perimeter CI/CD and shared services.
snakes.prevent: Run VPC-SC perimeters in Dry-Run mode (`spec`) and analyze `vpcServiceControlsUniqueIdentifier` dry-run violation logs before enforcing.
snakes.detect: Monitor Cloud Audit Logs with `metadata.dryRun = true` and `status.code = 7` (PERMISSION_DENIED) in Cloud Logging.
snakes.recover: Use the `vpcServiceControlsUniqueIdentifier` from the audit log to craft a least-privilege Ingress rule allowing the CI/CD service account and source project.
snakes.docLabel: VPC Service Controls Dry Run Mode
snakes.q: How should you safely design and roll out a new VPC Service Controls perimeter without causing production outages?
opts: Grant `allUsers` access in an ingress rule so nothing is ever blocked
Configure the perimeter in Dry-Run mode first, inspect Cloud Audit Logs for dry-run violations using the `vpcServiceControlsUniqueIdentifier`, add required ingress/egress rules, and then enforce
Disable Cloud Audit Logs so VPC-SC errors are suppressed
snakes.why: Dry-Run mode logs simulated perimeter blocks without dropping live traffic, letting teams discover legitimate cross-project flows safely.

snakes.title: Overbroad VPC-SC Egress Rule Allowed External Exfiltration
snakes.quip: "To fix a third-party data transfer error quickly, an admin added a VPC-SC Egress rule allowing `ANY_IDENTITY` to write to `resources: ['*']` on `storage.googleapis.com`. Neutralized the perimeter's data exfiltration protection for Cloud Storage, allowing compromised insiders to `gcloud storage cp` sensitive data to any external bucket."
snakes.tip: An egress rule to `resources: ['*']` with broad identities punches a hole straight through your VPC Service Controls perimeter.
snakes.prevent: Scope VPC-SC egress rules strictly to specific `serviceAccount:` identities, exact external project numbers (`projects/123456`), and specific methods.
snakes.detect: SCC `VPC_SC_PERIMETER_WEAK_EGRESS` posture checks and Policy Analyzer reviews of perimeter specs.
snakes.recover: Replace wildcard egress targets with explicit partner project numbers and dedicated transfer service accounts.
snakes.q: Why is configuring `resources: ['*']` with `identityType: ANY_IDENTITY` in a VPC Service Controls egress rule dangerous?
opts: It blocks all internal traffic within the same VPC subnet
It forces all Compute Engine VMs to reboot immediately
It allows any principal inside the perimeter to copy data from protected services into any external, attacker-controlled Google Cloud project
snakes.why: VPC-SC egress rules must restrict both the caller identity and the destination project list; wildcard resources defeat exfiltration prevention.

snakes.title: Private VMs Routed Google API Traffic via Public Cloud NAT
snakes.quip: "Workloads in an isolated subnet called `*.googleapis.com` without DNS CNAME routing to `restricted.googleapis.com`, sending traffic out through public Cloud NAT IPs instead. VPC-SC rejected requests because traffic arrived from unexpected public NAT egress IPs rather than private VPC internal access context, and saturated NAT gateways."
snakes.tip: Configure Private Google Access with a private Cloud DNS zone for `googleapis.com` resolving to `199.36.153.4/30` (`restricted.googleapis.com`) and explicit next-hop default gateway routes.
snakes.prevent: Automate Private DNS zones for `googleapis.com` and `gcr.io`/`pkg.dev` pointing to `199.36.153.4/30` in Shared VPC Terraform modules.
snakes.detect: Cloud NAT high bandwidth metrics toward Google IP ranges and VPC-SC audit logs showing external IP callers.
snakes.recover: Add the `199.36.153.4/30` route to the default internet gateway and create the `googleapis.com` private DNS zone resolving to `restricted.googleapis.com`.
snakes.q: How do you ensure private VMs without external IPs reach Google Cloud APIs over Google's internal network rather than consuming Cloud NAT or failing VPC-SC checks?
opts: Enable Private Google Access on the subnet, create a Private Cloud DNS zone for `googleapis.com` pointing to `restricted.googleapis.com` (`199.36.153.4/30`), and route `199.36.153.4/30` to the default internet gateway
Assign a public static IP address to every database VM
Disable TLS certificate verification in the Google Cloud SDK
snakes.why: Private Google Access paired with `restricted.googleapis.com` DNS resolution keeps API traffic internal and VPC-SC compliant without traversing Cloud NAT.

snakes.title: Cloud Armor WAF Rules Left in Preview Mode During Credential Stuffing
snakes.quip: "The team authored Cloud Armor rate-limiting and OWASP SQLi rules two months ago but left the `preview` flag enabled on every rule. During a 1.8M-request credential stuffing and SQLi campaign, Cloud Armor logged every match as `preview_deny` while forwarding 100% of malicious traffic to the backend."
snakes.tip: Preview mode logs what a Cloud Armor rule would do without blocking traffic; verify logs and disable preview mode to enforce protection.
snakes.prevent: Include automated CI policy checks that verify critical Cloud Armor rules have `preview: false` after the initial tuning window.
snakes.detect: Alert on spikes in `jsonPayload.enforcedSecurityPolicy.outcome = 'ACCEPT'` where `previewSecurityPolicy.outcome = 'DENY'` in HTTP Load Balancer logs.
snakes.recover: Uncheck Preview Mode (`--no-preview`) on the validated Cloud Armor rules to immediately block matching attack traffic at the edge.
snakes.q: What happens when a Google Cloud Armor security policy rule has Preview Mode enabled?
opts: Cloud Armor blocks 50% of matching requests at random
Matching requests are logged in Cloud Logging with the preview action outcome, but the rule is NOT enforced and traffic continues to be evaluated or allowed through
The rule is automatically promoted to enforced mode after 10 minutes
snakes.why: Preview mode is strictly for non-disruptive testing and logging; traffic is not blocked until preview mode is turned off.

snakes.title: Attackers Bypassed Cloud Armor by Hitting Backend Public IPs Directly
snakes.quip: "Application VMs behind a Global External Application Load Balancer retained ephemeral public IPs and a VPC firewall rule allowing `tcp:80,443` from `0.0.0.0/0`. Attackers discovered the origin VM IPs via historical certificate transparency logs and bypassed Cloud Armor WAF and IAP completely."
snakes.tip: Edge WAF and IAP protections are useless if attackers can connect directly to your backend VMs or NEGs over the public internet.
snakes.prevent: Remove public IPs from backend VMs and restrict ingress firewall rules exclusively to Google Front End (GFE) proxy and health-check ranges (`130.211.0.0/22` and `35.191.0.0/16`).
snakes.detect: SCC `OPEN_FIREWALL` / `LOAD_BALANCED_VM_PUBLIC_IP` findings and VPC Flow Logs showing non-GFE source IPs hitting backend instances.
snakes.recover: Update VPC ingress firewall rules to allow only `130.211.0.0/22` and `35.191.0.0/16` to target backend tags/service accounts, and remove external IPs from backend VMs.
snakes.q: How do you prevent attackers from bypassing Google Cloud Armor and connecting directly to Compute Engine backends behind a Global External Application Load Balancer?
opts: Change the backend web server port from 80 to 8080 while keeping `0.0.0.0/0` open
Add a `Robots.txt` file asking attackers to use the load balancer IP
Remove external IPs from backend VMs and configure VPC ingress firewall rules to allow traffic ONLY from Google's GFE/health-check ranges (`130.211.0.0/22` and `35.191.0.0/16`)
snakes.why: Restricting VPC ingress to Google Front End proxy ranges (`130.211.0.0/22`, `35.191.0.0/16`) and removing public IPs forces all traffic through Cloud Armor.

snakes.title: Unthrottled `/api/checkout` Endpoint Exhausted Vertex AI & DB Quota
snakes.quip: "A public promotional API endpoint had no Cloud Armor `throttle` or `rate_based_ban` rule configured. Automated scalper bots sent 80,000 requests/minute per IP, exhausting downstream database connection pools and racking up huge API bills."
snakes.tip: Always protect expensive public and authentication endpoints with Cloud Armor `rate_based_ban` or `throttle` rules keyed by client IP, header, or session cookie.
snakes.prevent: Deploy Cloud Armor rate-based ban rules (`enforce-on-key=IP` or `XFF-IP`) and integrate reCAPTCHA Enterprise challenge actions for suspicious bot scores.
snakes.detect: Cloud Monitoring 429/503 backend latency spikes and Cloud Armor telemetry per-IP request volume.
snakes.recover: Attach an emergency Cloud Armor `rate_based_ban` rule banning offending IPs for 600 seconds when exceeding threshold RPM.
snakes.q: What is the difference between a `throttle` action and a `rate_based_ban` action in Google Cloud Armor?
opts: `throttle` drops excess requests only while the client stays above the rate threshold, whereas `rate_based_ban` blocks all requests from the client for a configured ban duration (`ban_duration_sec`) once the threshold is crossed
`throttle` encrypts traffic while `rate_based_ban` decrypts traffic
`rate_based_ban` permanently deletes the client's DNS records
snakes.why: `rate_based_ban` enforces a penalty lockout period (`ban_duration_sec`) after a burst threshold is breached, stopping sustained bot scraping.

snakes.title: Privileged Pod with hostPath Mount Escaped to GKE Worker Node
snakes.quip: "A debugging DaemonSet was deployed with `privileged: true` and a `hostPath: /` volume mount in a GKE cluster without Pod Security Standards enforced. An attacker who exploited a web vulnerability in the pod mounted the node's root filesystem, stole kubelet credentials, and lateral-moved across the cluster."
snakes.tip: Never allow `privileged: true`, `hostPID`, `hostNetwork`, or `hostPath` mounts for application workloads; enforce Pod Security Standards (`restricted` or `baseline`).
snakes.prevent: Enforce Kubernetes Pod Security Admission (`pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted`) or Policy Controller constraints across all application namespaces.
snakes.detect: Container Threat Detection `ContainerEscape` / `AddedBinaryExecuted` findings and GKE Security Posture dashboard alerts.
snakes.recover: Isolate the affected node pool, cordoning and draining compromised nodes, rotate cluster credentials, and redeploy with `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` and `restricted` Pod Security Standard.
snakes.q: How do you prevent developers from deploying privileged containers or `hostPath` volume mounts in a production GKE cluster?
opts: Set the container CPU request to `100m`
Enforce the Kubernetes built-in Pod Security Admission controller with the `restricted` (or `baseline`) profile on namespaces, or apply Policy Controller / Gatekeeper constraints
Use a `:latest` Docker image tag
snakes.why: Pod Security Admission (`restricted` profile) and Policy Controller block pods requesting `privileged: true`, `hostPath`, or root execution at admission.

snakes.title: Deploying Mutable `:latest` Tags Bypassed Vulnerability Quarantine
snakes.quip: "Kubernetes manifests referenced `us-docker.pkg.dev/prod/app/web:latest` instead of an immutable `@sha256` digest, with Binary Authorization disabled. An unverified debug build pushed to `:latest` overwrote the production image tag and got pulled into production during a node scale-up event."
snakes.tip: Mutable tags like `:latest` can point to different binaries at any moment; always deploy by immutable `@sha256` digest verified by Binary Authorization.
snakes.prevent: Enable Artifact Registry immutable image tags or require `@sha256:` digests with Binary Authorization attestation enforcement.
snakes.detect: Artifact Analysis CVE alerts and GKE audit logs showing pod image pulls using mutable tags without digest pinning.
snakes.recover: Pin deployment manifests to the last verified `@sha256` digest, roll back the Deployment, and enable Binary Authorization on the cluster.
snakes.q: Why does Binary Authorization recommend deploying container images referenced by `@sha256:` digest rather than a mutable tag like `:v1` or `:latest`?
opts: Kubernetes cannot pull images that use tags shorter than 64 characters
`@sha256:` digests compress container layers to zero bytes
Attestations are cryptographically bound to the immutable content hash (`@sha256:`), whereas a mutable tag can be overwritten to point to an unverified image
snakes.why: Cryptographic attestations sign an exact immutable image digest; mutating a tag breaks the guarantee that the running code matches what was scanned.

snakes.title: GKE Control Plane Endpoint Left Open to 0.0.0.0/0 Without Authorized Networks
snakes.quip: "A production GKE cluster was provisioned with a public control plane endpoint and Control Plane Authorized Networks disabled. External scanners continuously probed the Kubernetes API server (`:443`), and a leaked developer kubeconfig token was used from an external Tor exit node."
snakes.tip: Restrict GKE control plane access using DNS-based endpoint + IAM/Access Context Manager or private IP + Authorized Networks via a bastion/IAP tunnel.
snakes.prevent: Enforce Organization Policy `constraints/ainotebooks` / GKE Policy Controller rules requiring Private Clusters and Control Plane Authorized Networks.
snakes.detect: SCC `OPEN_CLUSTER_ENDPOINT` / `AUTHORIZED_NETWORKS_DISABLED` findings and GKE `kube-apiserver` audit logs from unknown external IPs.
snakes.recover: Enable Control Plane Authorized Networks (or private endpoint only) and access the cluster via Connect Gateway or an IAP-secured bastion host.
snakes.q: How should administrators securely connect to a private GKE control plane without exposing the Kubernetes API server to `0.0.0.0/0`?
opts: Disable public unrestricted access on the control plane and connect via Connect Gateway, an IAP-tunneled bastion host, or private VPC peasant/VPN networks in Authorized Networks
Expose the Kubernetes API on unauthenticated HTTP port 8080
Share a single static `cluster-admin` client certificate inside a public Slack channel
snakes.why: Private control plane endpoints combined with Connect Gateway or IAP-secured authorized networks eliminate internet exposure of `kube-apiserver`.

snakes.title: Scheduled Destruction of Active CMEK Key Version Used by Production Archives
snakes.quip: "During a cleanup sprint, an admin scheduled destruction on an older Cloud KMS key version without checking if historical BigQuery snapshots and GCS Coldline objects still depended on it. Because asymmetric/older non-re-encrypted objects were still wrapped with that key version, 14 TB of regulatory archive blobs became permanently undecryptable once the destruction window expired."
snakes.tip: Once a Cloud KMS key version passes its scheduled destruction window, the key material is cryptographically erased forever and encrypted data is permanently unrecoverable.
snakes.prevent: Set the Cloud KMS minimum scheduled destruction duration to 30+ days, restrict `cloudkms.cryptoKeyVersions.destroy` via IAM Deny, and check Key Usage tracking in KMS before scheduling destruction.
snakes.detect: Configure high-priority Cloud Monitoring / Log-based alerts on `ScheduleCryptoKeyVersionDestruction` audit events and SCC `KMS_KEY_SCHEDULED_FOR_DESTRUCTION` notifications.
snakes.recover: Call `RestoreCryptoKeyVersion` (`gcloud kms keys versions restore`) immediately BEFORE the scheduled destruction window (minimum 24 hours) expires!
snakes.docLabel: Destroy and Restore KMS Key Versions
snakes.q: What safeguard does Cloud KMS provide when `DestroyCryptoKeyVersion` is called on a Customer-Managed Encryption Key (CMEK)?
opts: Google Support keeps a plaintext backup of destroyed keys for 10 years

The key version enters the `DESTROY_scheduled` state for a configurable waiting period (24 hours by default, up to 120 days), during which data access fails loudly and admins can call `RestoreCryptoKeyVersion`
The key is destroyed in 5 milliseconds with no waiting period
snakes.why: The `DESTROY_SCHEDULED` state disables decryption immediately (surfacing any unseen dependencies in logs) while allowing full restoration before the timer expires.

snakes.title: Raw Credit Card PANs and SSNs Printed to Cloud Logging in Debug Mode
snakes.quip: "A payment microservice enabled verbose request body logging during an incident, writing cleartext credit card numbers and SSNs into `_Default` Cloud Logging buckets. Hundreds of engineers with `roles/logging.viewer` gained access to regulated PCI/PII data in violation of PCI-DSS scope."
snakes.tip: Never log raw request bodies containing PII/PCI; inspect and redact sensitive fields before logging or via Sensitive Data Protection.
snakes.prevent: Use structured logging filters in application middleware and run Sensitive Data Protection (Cloud DLP) inspection templates on log sinks and storage.
snakes.detect: Sensitive Data Protection automatic discovery profiles and log inspection jobs alerting on `CREDIT_CARD_NUMBER` and `US_SOCIAL_SECURITY_NUMBER` infoTypes.
snakes.recover: Disable verbose payload logging, configure Log Sink exclusion/redaction filters, and purge or restrict IAM access (`Log Views`) on the affected Log Bucket.
snakes.q: How can you prevent sensitive PII fields in Cloud Logging from being visible to general developers who only need application error logs?
opts: Make the `_Default` log bucket world-readable
Email the raw log files to every developer daily instead of using Cloud Logging
Redact or tokenize sensitive fields before ingestion using Sensitive Data Protection / OpenTelemetry processors, and use fine-grained Cloud Logging Log Views with IAM Conditions to restrict access
snakes.why: Combining pre-ingestion redaction (Sensitive Data Protection) with restricted Log Views keeps regulated data out of general developer reach.

snakes.title: Regulated Healthcare Bucket Created with Default Google-Managed Keys Instead of CMEK
snakes.quip: "A data scientist created a new staging Cloud Storage bucket via CLI without specifying `--default-encryption-key`, bypassing the compliance requirement for customer-managed keys. Failed the quarterly HIPAA/HITRUST compliance audit because key rotation and revocation were not under customer KMS control."
snakes.tip: Relying on manual CLI flags for CMEK fails at scale; enforce CMEK via Organization Policy constraints.
snakes.detect: Security Command Center compliance violations for CIS / HIPAA / PCI-DSS benchmarks and Cloud Asset Inventory encryption posture queries.
snakes.recover: Apply the CMEK key to the bucket, rewrite existing objects (`gcloud storage objects update --encryption-key`) so they are re-wrapped under CMEK, and enable the Org Policy constraint.
snakes.q: Which Organization Policy constraint forces new resources in specified services (such as Cloud Storage, BigQuery, and Compute Engine) to be created ONLY with Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK)?
opts: `constraints/gcp.restrictNonCmekServices`
`constraints/compute.vmExternalIpAccess`
`constraints/iam.disableAuditLoggingExemption`
snakes.why: Enforcing `constraints/gcp.restrictNonCmekServices` rejects API calls that attempt to create resources in listed services without a valid Cloud KMS CMEK key.

snakes.title: Data Access Audit Logs Were Disabled During Data Exfiltration Investigation
snakes.quip: "After revoking a compromised contractor account, the IR team tried to determine which specific objects in a sensitive Cloud Storage bucket the contractor had downloaded. Because `DATA_READ` and `DATA_WRITE` Cloud Audit Logs were never enabled on Cloud Storage, there was zero forensic record of which files were accessed."
snakes.tip: Admin Activity logs are always on, but Data Access (`DATA_READ`/`DATA_WRITE`) logs are disabled by default for most services and must be explicitly enabled for critical datasets.
snakes.prevent: Enable `DATA_READ` and `DATA_WRITE` Cloud Audit Logs on folders/projects containing sensitive data and route them to a locked, centralized Log Bucket.
snakes.detect: SCC `AUDIT_LOGGING_DISABLED` posture findings and Event Threat Detection coverage checks.
snakes.recover: Enable `DATA_READ` and `DATA_WRITE` audit log configurations in IAM Audit Logs for critical services (`storage.googleapis.com`, `bigquery.googleapis.com`, `cloudkms.googleapis.com`).
snakes.q: Why could an incident response team see when a Cloud Storage bucket was created (`storage.buckets.create`), but NOT see which objects an attacker downloaded (`storage.objects.get`)?
opts: Cloud Storage does not support HTTPS logging

Admin Activity audit logs are enabled by default, whereas Data Access audit logs (`DATA_READ` and `DATA_WRITE`) are disabled by default for most services to control log volume and must be explicitly enabled
Admin Activity logs are deleted every 30 seconds
snakes.why: To capture `DATA_READ` and `DATA_WRITE` events for forensics and Event Threat Detection, you must explicitly enable Data Access audit logs on target services.

snakes.title: Compromised Project Owner Deleted Project-Level Log Sinks & Modified Buckets
snakes.quip: "Audit logs were stored inside each individual application project rather than routed via an Organization-level aggregated sink to a locked security project. An attacker who compromised a project admin role deleted the local log sink and shortened retention to hide lateral movement."
snakes.tip: Centralize audit logs using an Organization-level aggregated sink (`--include-children`) writing to a dedicated SecOps project with Locked Log Bucket retention.
snakes.prevent: Configure an Organization-level aggregated Log Sink to a separate security project and lock the destination Log Bucket retention policy.
snakes.detect: Admin Activity audit log alert on `logging.sinks.delete`, `logging.sinks.update`, or `logging.buckets.update`.
snakes.recover: Restore the sink configuration via Terraform, enable a Locked Log Bucket in an isolated SecOps project, and attach an IAM Deny policy protecting logging resources.
snakes.q: How do you architect Cloud Audit Logging so that even a compromised Project Owner in an application project cannot delete or alter the audit trail?
opts: Store audit logs as editable `.csv` files on the application VM's `/tmp` directory
Give every user in the company `roles/logging.admin`
Create an Organization-level aggregated Log Sink (`includeChildren: true`) that routes logs before project-level exclusions into a separate SecOps project's Log Bucket with a Locked retention policy
snakes.why: Intercepting logs at the Organization sink level and storing them in an isolated project's Locked Log Bucket prevents project-level admins from tampering with evidence.

snakes.title: 14,000 Unfiltered Low-Severity Dev Findings Buried a Critical Prod Reverse Shell
snakes.quip: "The SOC forwarded every raw informational finding from 80 sandbox projects into the primary pager channel without Attack Exposure scoring or mute rules. On-call engineers muted the pager channel due to noise, missing a high-severity Container Threat Detection `ReverseShell` alert in production for 6 hours."
snakes.tip: Use SCC Attack Exposure Scores, High-Value Resource definitions, and dynamic Mute Rules for non-production sandboxes so critical runtime threats page immediately.
snakes.prevent: Define High-Value Resource Sets in SCC, apply Mute Rules for non-prod informational findings, and route only `CRITICAL`/`HIGH` ETD/CTD runtime threats and top Attack Exposure findings to PagerDuty.
snakes.detect: Track SOC Mean Time to Acknowledge (MTTA) and alert signal-to-noise ratio in Google SecOps.
snakes.recover: Separate notification configs: route active runtime detections (ETD/CTD) to immediate SOAR/PagerDuty response and posture findings to ticketing queues ranked by Attack Exposure Score.
snakes.docLabel: Mute Findings in Security Command Center
snakes.q: How should security teams prevent low-priority posture findings in sandbox projects from drowning out active breach detections in Security Command Center?
opts: Use SCC dynamic Mute Rules and folder filters for sandbox posture noise, define High-Value Resource Sets for Attack Path prioritization, and route runtime Event/Container Threat Detection alerts to high-priority incident channels
Disable Security Command Center across the entire organization
Delete all production projects so only sandbox projects remain
snakes.why: Separating high-confidence runtime threat detections (ETD/CTD) from posture backlog items and using Attack Exposure Scores eliminates alert fatigue.

shields.title: Org Policy `iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation`
shields.tip: Preventing static key creation at the org policy layer eliminates the #1 cause of cloud credential leaks.

shields.title: Domain Restricted Sharing (`iam.allowedPolicyMemberDomains`)
shields.quip: "Locked IAM bindings to your corporate Google Workspace customer ID via `constraints/iam.allowedPolicyMemberDomains`."
shields.tip: Enforce Domain Restricted Sharing so no principal outside your trusted organization domains can be added to IAM policies.

shields.title: Automated Least-Privilege with IAM Recommender
shields.quip: "Reviewed 90-day permission usage telemetry via Policy Intelligence IAM Recommender and pruned 1,400 unused role bindings."
shields.tip: Use IAM Recommender and Policy Analyzer continuously to right-size over-granted roles down to least privilege.

shields.title: VPC-SC Dry-Run Perimeter & Violation Monitor
shields.quip: "Deployed a shadow Dry-Run VPC Service Controls perimeter across all staging and production folders with automated log dashboards."
shields.tip: Always test perimeter expansions and ingress/egress edits in VPC-SC Dry-Run mode before enforcing.

shields.title: Org Policy `compute.vmExternalIpAccess` Deny All
shields.quip: "Enforced `constraints/compute.vmExternalIpAccess` denying public external IP addresses on all Compute Engine VMs."
shields.tip: Block direct external IPs on VMs by default and use IAP TCP forwarding for administrative SSH/RDP access.

shields.title: IAP TCP Forwarding for Bastion-Free SSH
shields.quip: "Replaced public bastion hosts with Identity-Aware Proxy TCP forwarding (`gcloud compute ssh --tunnel-through-iap`) restricted to `35.235.240.0/20`."
shields.tip: Allow SSH ingress only from IAP's `35.235.240.0/20` range and require `roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor`.

shields.title: Cloud Armor + reCAPTCHA Enterprise Bot Defense
shields.quip: "Integrated reCAPTCHA Enterprise fraud scores directly into Cloud Armor edge security policies for login and checkout routes."
shields.tip: Combine Cloud Armor WAF with reCAPTCHA Enterprise tokens to stop automated botnets without hurting human conversion.

shields.title: Modern TLS 1.2+ SSL Policy on Load Balancers
shields.quip: "Attached a `MODERN` / `RESTRICTED` minimum TLS 1.2 SSL Policy to all external HTTPS Load Balancers, disabling weak TLS 1.0/1.1 ciphers."
shields.tip: Use a managed SSL Policy with `RESTRICTED` or `MODERN` profile and minimum TLS 1.2 on every external load balancer.

shields.title: Automated Artifact Analysis On-Push CVE Scanning
shields.quip: "Enabled Artifact Analysis continuous container scanning on Artifact Registry to flag critical OS and language package CVEs immediately on push."
shields.tip: Scan every container push in Artifact Registry and gate promotions on zero fixable Critical CVEs.

shields.title: GKE Sandbox (gVisor) Kernel Isolation for Untrusted Code
shields.quip: "Isolated multi-tenant and third-party plugin pods inside GKE Sandbox (`runtimeClassName: gvisor`) node pools."
shields.tip: Use GKE Sandbox (gVisor) to add a second layer of syscall isolation for untrusted or multi-tenant workloads.

shields.title: Anthos / GKE Policy Controller CIS Guardrails
shields.quip: "Activated GKE Policy Controller with the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark constraint bundle in admission and audit modes."
shields.tip: Enforce declarative OPA Gatekeeper / Policy Controller constraints in CI and cluster admission.

shields.title: Automated 90-Day Cloud KMS Key Rotation
shields.quip: "Configured automatic 90-day key rotation schedules across all symmetric CMEK CryptoKeys with 30-day destruction windows."
shields.tip: Enable automatic key rotation on symmetric Cloud KMS keys so new writes always use fresh key material.

shields.title: Confidential VMs & Confidential GKE Nodes (AMD SEV / Intel TDX)
shields.quip: "Deployed sensitive analytics and payment processing workloads on Confidential VMs with hardware memory encryption in use."
shields.tip: Use Confidential Computing (Confidential VMs / Confidential GKE) to protect sensitive data in-use in memory, complementing encryption at-rest and in-transit.

shields.title: Organization-Wide Public Access Prevention & Uniform Bucket Access
shields.quip: "Enforced `storage.publicAccessPrevention` and `storage.uniformBucketLevelAccess` across every folder in the organization."
shields.tip: Combine Uniform Bucket-Level Access with Organization-enforced Public Access Prevention to simplify and harden Cloud Storage security.

shields.title: Immutable Locked Log Bucket for SecOps Audit Trail
shields.quip: "Locked the 400-day retention policy on the centralized Organization Audit Log Bucket in the isolated SecOps project."
shields.tip: Lock retention on centralized security Log Buckets to guarantee tamper-proof forensic evidence.

shields.title: SCC Security Posture Drift Detection & IaC Validation
shields.quip: "Deployed an Organization Security Posture YAML policy monitoring live drift against SHA-pinned Org Policies and SHA-validated Terraform plans."
shields.tip: Use Security Command Center Security Posture service to codify, validate in CI, and continuously monitor drift on org policies and SHA detectors.
